# Regulatory Dossier: Publishing an Android App With an Autonomous Web-Browsing and File-Creating Agent

**Prepared for:** Mobile product, engineering, legal, and trust-and-safety teams
**Scope:** Google Play distribution of an Android application containing an autonomous AI agent capable of web browsing and on-device file creation, with attention to required user disclosures, opt-out mechanisms, in-app report buttons, privacy policy clauses, and data-protection obligations governing on-device file access and logging.
**Status:** Working compliance dossier. Policy text and deadlines change frequently; every cited source should be re-verified against the live page before submission and again before each release.

---

## 1. Executive Summary

An Android app that deploys an autonomous agent with web browsing and file creation is treated by regulators and by Google as a **high-risk AI feature**, not a routine utility. Three regimes interact:

1. **Google Play policy** — the app store gatekeeper. It enforces its own Generative AI Prohibited Content policy, Deceptive Behavior rules, and a strict requirement that your Data safety form and privacy policy accurately describe agent-driven data collection and file access.
2. **EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)** — transparency and prohibitions provisions phase in across 2025 and 2026, including the obligation to disclose that the user is interacting with an AI system and to machine-mark synthetic content.
3. **Data protection law (GDPR, ePrivacy, and analogous frameworks)** — governs on-device file access, telemetry, and agent action logs, particularly where logs capture file contents, browsing history, or prompt history.

The practical compliance posture for launch is: **conspicuous first-run disclosure, a persistent "this is an AI" indicator, granular opt-outs for autonomous actions, a visible report/fallback control in every agent surface, an accurate Data safety form, and a privacy policy that specifically names agent logs, file access, and web browsing traffic.**

---

## 2. Google Play Store Requirements

### 2.1 Generative AI policy and prohibited content

Google operates a dedicated **Generative AI Prohibited Content** policy for apps using generative models. Its core requirements map almost directly onto agent features:

- Apps with generative AI features must **implement robust content filters** to block responses covering at least these categories: violent, sexual, hateful, dangerous, medically misleading, and harass/threat content.
- Developers must provide **in-app reporting mechanisms** so users can flag offensive or policy-violating output. The report affordance must be reasonably discoverable, not buried behind multiple screens.
- Developers must **disclose the presence of generative AI features** in the app listing and in-app so users are not misled about what is human-authored versus machine-generated.
- Apps whose primary purpose is generating content in these prohibited categories, or that facilitate evasion of content safeguards, are removed from the store.

**Source:** https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14755907?hl=en (Generative AI prohibited content policy)

### 2.2 Deceptive Behavior and AI misrepresentation

Google Play's **Deceptive Behavior** policy prohibits apps that misrepresent their functionality or deceive users. For an autonomous agent this means:

- You may not describe the agent as "fully autonomous" or "acts on your behalf without supervision" unless the description matches actual behavior.
- If the agent performs web browsing, downloads files, or creates/edits files, the listing and onboarding must say so plainly.
- Preloaded or automatically triggered behavior (such as the agent beginning a browsing task without an explicit user command) must be disclosed at first run.

**Source:** https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9898816?hl=en (Deceptive behavior policy)

### 2.3 Data safety form and permissions

The **Data safety** form in Play Console is a legal-adjacent attestation. For an agent with browsing and file creation you must declare:

- **Data types:** browsing history, web pages viewed, files created/modified, app activity, and any prompts or model inputs that contain personal data.
- **Whether data is collected and whether it is shared**, including with model providers (e.g., cloud LLM APIs).
- **Encryption in transit** (TLS) and **data deletion** options offered to users.
- Whether data is **ephemeral** or retained in logs.

**File access:** If the agent writes or reads user-visible files, request `READ_MEDIA_*` / `MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` only where the onboarding explains why. Scoped storage is preferred; broad storage access triggers additional Play scrutiny. Recent Play data safety policy versions require disclosure of **data access that occurs in the background**, which an autonomous agent commonly does.

**Source:** https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9842480?hl=en (Data safety)

### 2.4 Target audience, Families, and age ratings

If the app is available to minors, additional rules apply: the app must not enable unrestricted web browsing for children, and any agent chat must have heightened content filtering. Otherwise, submit an age rating questionnaire that honestly reflects agent-driven open-web access; under-disclosure creates takedown risk.

**Source:** https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9858744?hl=en

### 2.5 Remote work / app functionality updates

Agent behavior driven by server-side prompts or model changes must be disclosed where it materially changes data handling. Google's policies treat **material changes to data collection requiring re-consent** as mandatory; update your privacy policy and re-prompt consent before rollout.

---

## 3. EU AI Act — Provisions Taking Effect This Cycle

The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) entered into force on **1 August 2024**, with a staggered application calendar. The provisions most relevant to a browsing, file-creating agent are the **prohibitions** and the **transparency obligations**.

### 3.1 Prohibitions (applied from 2 February 2025)

Article 5 bans, among others: subliminal manipulation, exploitation of vulnerabilities, social scoring, untargeted facial-image scraping, and certain predictive policing uses. A consumer agent is unlikely to trip these unless it manipulates users or profiles them on sensitive traits. **Keep agent task prompts free of manipulation patterns.**

**Source:** https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/5/ (Article 5 text)

### 3.2 AI literacy (applied from 2 February 2025)

Providers and deployers must take measures to ensure a **sufficient level of AI literacy** among staff and operators. For a small team shipping an agent, document internal AI-literacy training (session dates, attendees, topics) — auditors increasingly ask for this artifact.

**Source:** https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/4/ (Article 4 — AI literacy)

### 3.3 Transparency obligations: Article 50 (applied from 2 August 2026)

This is the central requirement for your product:

- **Article 50(1):** Systems interacting directly with natural persons must be designed so that persons are **informed they are interacting with an AI system**, unless that is obvious from the circumstances and the context of use. For a chat-style agent, this is never "obvious" — carry a persistent, non-hidden indicator.
- **Article 50(4):** AI-generated or manipulated **content that is appreciable as text** must be **machine-readable and marked as artificially generated** in a format that is interoperable, robust, and reliable (watermarking/metadata), where feasible.
- **Article 50(5):** Providers of systems generating deepfakes must disclose the content is artificially generated.

**Source:** https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/50/ (Article 50 — transparency)

### 3.4 General-purpose AI model obligations (applied from 2 August 2025)

If you build on a third-party foundation model, you are a **deployer**, not a GPAI provider — but you must contractually ensure your model supplier supplies you with the documentation, copyright policy, and **sufficiently detailed summary of training content** needed for your own downstream disclosures. If you fine-tune and resell the model, obligations may shift onto you.

**Source:** https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/53/ (Article 53 — GPAI provider obligations)

### 3.5 Penalties

- Prohibitions/AI literacy breaches: up to **€15 million or 3% of global annual turnover**.
- Transparency (Art. 50) breaches: up to **€7.5 million or 1%**.
- Supplying incorrect information to authorities: **€7.5 million / 1%**.

**Source:** https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/99/ (Article 99 — penalties)

### 3.6 Classification caution

Most consumer task agents are **non-high-risk** (no Annex III use case such as employment, credit, or critical infrastructure). If your agent is later extended into CV screening, credit decisions, or education assessment, re-classify immediately — high-risk obligations attach from **2 August 2026** (Annex III) and **2 August 2027** (Annex I products).

**Source:** https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/annex/3/ (Annex III high-risk uses)

---

## 4. Data Protection: On-Device File Access and Logging

### 4.1 GDPR principles applicable to agent logs

Under GDPR, agent action logs are **personal data** whenever they contain identifiers, file paths, URLs, or prompt content tied to a person:

- **Art. 5(1)(c) data minimisation:** log the *event* (task ID, action type, target domain, success/failure) rather than the file contents or full page text.
- **Art. 5(1)(e) storage limitation:** define retention. A practical default is 30–90 days for raw action logs, longer for abuse-prevention hashes.
- **Art. 6 lawful basis:** contract performance for core agent execution; **legitimate interests** for abuse detection — document a balancing test; **consent** for optional telemetry and for any data used to improve models.
- **Art. 13/14 transparency:** your privacy policy must state categories of data, purposes, retention, recipients (including the LLM provider), and rights.
- **Art. 30 records of processing:** maintain a ROPA entry covering "agent execution logging" and "web browsing proxy."
- **Art. 32 security:** encrypt logs at rest; scrub tokens, cookies, and session headers captured during browsing before persistence.
- **Art. 35 DPIA:** almost certainly required — the processing combines systematic web tracking, file access, and automated decision-support. Do the DPIA before launch.
- **Art. 22:** if the agent's output produces legal or similarly significant effects on a user, provide human intervention and the right to contest.

**Source:** https://gdpr-info.eu/art-5-gdpr/ (Art. 5 principles); https://gdpr-info.eu/art-35-gdpr/ (DPIA)

### 4.2 On-device file access specifically

- Read/write only the **minimum directories** required; prefer the app-specific storage and the Storage Access Framework (SAF) document picker over blanket storage permissions.
- Every file write triggered autonomously must produce an **on-device action record the user can inspect** (what file, where, when, why).
- A "dry-run / preview" mode — where the agent shows the proposed file operation before executing — materially reduces both risk and your liability exposure.
- Do not transmit file contents to cloud model endpoints unless the user opted in and the transfer is disclosed in the Data safety form.

### 4.3 Browsing and ePrivacy

When the agent's browser sets or reads cookies/terminal-information, **ePrivacy Directive Art. 5(3)** consent requirements apply in the EEA in addition to GDPR. Disclose that the agent browses on the user's behalf and state whether tracking technologies are used for anything beyond the requested page load.

**Source:** https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A32002L0058

### 4.4 Children

If the app is directed to or likely to be accessed by children, GDPR Art. 8 consent gates and Google Play Families policy both apply; the combination of open web browsing and file creation for minors is a strong takedown trigger.

---

## 5. Required User Disclosures

| # | Disclosure | Where it must appear |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | "This app uses an AI agent that can browse websites and create files on your device." | Play listing short description, onboarding screen 1, settings |
| D2 | Persistent "AI" indicator on every agent output surface | Chat/agent UI header, per-response badge |
| D3 | Explanation that AI output may be inaccurate and user should verify | Onboarding, and adjacent to agent responses with a "Verify" link |
| D4 | Which third-party model provider receives prompts/data | Privacy policy + in-app "Data & AI" screen |
| D5 | Autonomous action notice: "The agent may act without asking each time; you can change this in Settings." | Onboarding + settings |
| D6 | File access notice with directory scope and a link to the action history | First file-write prompt and settings |
| D7 | Web browsing notice, including that the agent's requests originate from your servers or the device | Onboarding, privacy policy |
| D8 | Content-safety notice and how to report a violation | Near every agent response |
| D9 | EU AI Act Art. 50 statement: user is interacting with an AI system | Onboarding (EEA), persistent indicator |
| D10 | Age gate / eligibility statement | First run |

---

## 6. Opt-Out Mechanisms

Effective opt-outs must be **granular, persistent, revocable, and equal in prominence to the opt-in** (a dark-pattern-free default-off for optional telemetry is the safe posture under GDPR and under Google's deceptive-behavior rules).

1. **Autonomous execution toggle** — default: agent must confirm before each write/browse action; user may enable "auto-run." One tap to revert.
2. **Directory scope opt-out** — user selects which folders the agent may touch; "deny all" is always available.
3. **Web browsing opt-out** — disable browsing while keeping local file features, and vice versa.
4. **Telemetry / analytics opt-out** — default off for content-bearing logs; separate toggle from crash reporting.
5. **Model-improvement data sharing opt-out** — default off; must also be honored by your subprocessor.
6. **Cross-session memory opt-out** — delete stored conversation/plan history on demand and on uninstall.
7. **EU-specific AI consent** — Article 50 disclosure acceptance cannot be gated behind unrelated permissions.
8. **Account deletion** — required by Google Play; must delete agent logs server-side within the stated window.

**Source:** https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9842480?hl=en (data deletion requirements)

---

## 7. Report Buttons

Google's generative-AI policy requires in-app reporting. Implement:

- **Per-response report control** — a persistent overflow/report icon on every agent message, opening a category picker: (a) harmful/inappropriate content, (b) misinformation, (c) acted on my files without permission, (d) browsed to an inappropriate site, (e) other.
- **Global report entry** — Settings → "Report a problem," plus an always-visible control during agent task execution to **stop and report**.
- **Abuse contact** — an email or web form reachable without an account, as required for `abuse@` contactability by Google and by the DSA if the app is in scope as a platform.
- **SLA and escalation** — route reports to a triage queue; suspend the offending prompt template or tool permission on first credible report of unauthorized file writes.
- **Appeal path** — notify the user of outcome where feasible.

**Source:** https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14755907?hl=en; https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/10187672 (contact and policy compliance requirements)

---

## 8. Privacy Policy Clauses (required language areas)

Your privacy policy must include, at minimum, clauses covering:

1. **Agent description:** "Our app includes an autonomous AI agent that can perform web browsing and create, modify, or delete files on your device on your behalf."
2. **Categories of data collected:** prompts/conversations, agent task plans, action logs (including URLs visited and file paths touched), device identifiers, crash logs, and any uploaded documents.
3. **Purpose of processing:** task execution, safety enforcement, abuse prevention, model improvement (only if opted in), analytics.
4. **Legal basis:** contract performance; legitimate interests for security logging; consent for optional telemetry and model improvement.
5. **Recipients and subprocessors:** name the LLM/cloud provider(s), hosting provider, and analytics SDKs; state that prompts are transmitted to the model provider.
6. **Transfers:** mechanism for non-EEA transfers (SCCs / DPF), with link to safeguards.
7. **Retention:** separate periods for conversation history, action logs, and crash logs; state deletion triggers.
8. **On-device vs. cloud:** explicit statement of what stays local, what is uploaded.
9. **Automated decision-making:** reference to GDPR Art. 22 if applicable, and human review options.
10. **Rights:** access, rectification, erasure, portability, objection, withdrawal of consent, complaint to a supervisory authority.
11. **Children:** age requirements and COPPA/GDPR Art. 8 statements.
12. **Security:** encryption in transit and at rest, log redaction practices.
13. **Changes:** how material policy changes trigger re-consent.
14. **Contact:** DPO or privacy contact address.

**Sources:** https://gdpr-info.eu/art-13-gdpr/; https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9842480?hl=en

---

## 9. Pre-Launch Checklist

**Policy & store readiness**
- [ ] Read the live Generative AI prohibited content policy and confirm filters block all required categories (https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14755907)
- [ ] In-app report button present on every agent response; category picker wired to a triage queue
- [ ] Generative AI features disclosed in Play listing description and screenshots
- [ ] Deceptive-behavior review: every claim in the listing matches actual agent behavior (https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9898816)
- [ ] Data safety form updated: browsing history, files, prompts, background collection, encryption, sharing with model provider (https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9842480)
- [ ] Permissions requested are minimal; SAF used instead of broad storage access; justification written for each
- [ ] Age rating questionnaire completed honestly reflecting open-web access
- [ ] Account deletion path tested and functional within stated timeframe
- [ ] Target audience / Families designation verified

**EU AI Act readiness**
- [ ] Article 50(1) AI-interaction disclosure implemented and persistent (https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/50/)
- [ ] Machine-readable marking of generated text/metadata where feasible (Art. 50(4))
- [ ] AI-literacy training completed and documented for the team (Art. 4, https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/4/)
- [ ] Art. 5 prohibited-use screening documented (https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/5/)
- [ ] Model provider documentation obtained per Art. 53 (https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/53/)
- [ ] Annex III screening: confirm no high-risk classification (https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/annex/3/)
- [ ] Penalties exposure reviewed: up to €15M/3% and €7.5M/1% (https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/99/)

**Data protection**
- [ ] DPIA completed before launch (https://gdpr-info.eu/art-35-gdpr/)
- [ ] ROPA entry created for agent logging and browsing proxy (Art. 30)
- [ ] Lawful-basis analysis documented per purpose (Art. 6)
- [ ] Log retention defined (recommend ≤90 days raw) and automated purge in place
- [ ] Log scrubbing removes file contents, cookies, auth headers, and secrets (Art. 32)
- [ ] ePrivacy consent handled for any cookie/terminal-information access (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A32002L0058)
- [ ] Children's data pathways disabled or gated (GDPR Art. 8)

**UX: disclosures, opt-outs, reports**
- [ ] First-run disclosure D1–D10 delivered and acceptance logged
- [ ] Persistent "AI" indicator visible on all agent output
- [ ] Default is confirm-before-act; auto-run is opt-in and one tap to disable
- [ ] Directory scope selector with "deny all" option
- [ ] Independent toggles: browsing, telemetry, model-improvement sharing, memory — all default off where optional
- [ ] Agent action history screen showing every file write and URL visited, with undo
- [ ] Stop/report control available mid-task
- [ ] Privacy policy updated with all 14 clause areas from Section 8 and published at the required Play URL
- [ ] Re-consent flow tested for material policy changes
- [ ] Final end-to-end audit on a test device: agent behavior matches every disclosed claim

---

## 10. Conclusion

The compliance posture for a browsing, file-creating Android agent is **disclosure-first**: Google Play demands accurate listing and Data safety declarations plus in-app generative-AI reporting; the EU AI Act requires unmistakable AI-interaction disclosure (Art. 50) and documented AI literacy; GDPR demands minimised, time-bounded, encrypted agent logs backed by a DPIA. Ship with confirm-by-default execution, granular opt-outs, per-response report controls, and a privacy policy that names browsing, file access, and logging explicitly — then re-verify every cited policy page before submission, since these rules are actively changing.

# Local Android AI Agent — Modular Architecture Specification

**Version:** 1.0
**Runtime target:** Android 13+, on-device LLM (e.g. a 3B–8B quantized instruct model via llama.cpp / MLC / MediaPipe LLM Inference API), no cloud dependency required for the core loop.
**Scope:** Agent loop, token budgeting, tool-routing policy, error recovery, and fallback logic for four tools — `web_search`, `file_manager`, `calculator`, `settings_manager`.

---

## 1. Design goals and modular decomposition

The system is split into five independently replaceable modules. Each module communicates only through typed interfaces, so any module (especially the model itself) can be swapped without touching the others.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  UI / Voice Surface (Android Compose, accessibility aware)  │
└──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘
                           │ UserUtterance
┌──────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────┐
│  ORCHESTRATOR (Agent Loop)                                  │
│  - prompt assembly   - token budgeter   - stop-condition FSM│
└───────┬──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────┘
        │ ToolCall                     │ ModelOutput
┌───────▼───────────────┐   ┌──────────▼──────────────────────┐
│ TOOL ROUTER           │   │ MODEL ADAPTER (pluggable)       │
│ - schema validation   │   │ - local GGUF/OTF runtime        │
│ - arg repair          │   │ - JSON-constrained decoding     │
│ - dispatch + timeout  │   └─────────────────────────────────┘
│ - retry / backoff     │
└───────┬───────────────┘
        │ ToolRequest
┌───────▼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ TOOL HOST (sandboxed)                                       │
│  web_search │ file_manager │ calculator │ settings_manager  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Modularity here is the same principle used in prefabricated building systems: components are factory-specified against a contract, then composed on site. The Eames Office's modular system at Milan Design Week (https://coolhunting.com/design/the-eames-office-brings-a-modular-architecture-system-to-life-at-milan-design-week/) and Australia's modular remote-build program (https://www.architectureanddesign.com.au/features/a-new-high-for-modular-buildings-in-australia-s-remote-heart) both demonstrate the operational payoff — predefined interfaces, factory QA, and field-swappable units reduce failure surface. The same argument is made for modular EV charging infrastructure (https://www.allaboutcircuits.com/news/modular-architecture-the-key-to-reliable-ev-charging-infrastructure/), where the failure of one module must not take down the system: that is exactly the property we need when one tool faults mid-task. Parametric/panelised systems (https://www.parametric-architecture.com/10-modular-architecture-innovations-that-are-redefining-the-future-of-living/) and modular timber façade assemblies (https://www.archpaper.com/facades-toronto-aec-experts-discuss-innovations-in-prefabrication-and-modular-timber-design/) reinforce the pattern: standardised joints, explicit tolerances, and documented assembly sequences. In software terms: strict schemas, explicit budgets, documented retry sequences.

**Hard rules**

1. The model never executes anything. It only emits structured tool calls.
2. The Tool Router is the only component that touches Android APIs.
3. Every tool is individually disableable; disabling degrades the agent, it does not crash it.
4. All tool I/O passes JSON Schema validation *both* on the way out (arguments) and on the way in (results).

---

## 2. The prompt loop

### 2.1 Message lifecycle

The loop is a finite state machine with four states:

```
IDLE → PLANNING → ACTING → OBSERVING ─┐
                     ▲                │
                     └────────────────┘  (max N iterations)
PLANNING → DONE (final answer emitted)
any       → ERROR (hard failure, apology + partial result)
```

**Per-iteration sequence:**

1. **Assemble prompt.** Concatenate: system prompt → tool schemas (rendered as a compact text block, not raw JSON-Schema) → conversation history → scratchpad (observations).
2. **Budget check.** Compute available tokens (see §3). Truncate oldest observations first; never truncate the system prompt or the current user turn.
3. **Model call.** Sample with JSON-constrained decoding if available, otherwise sample normally and post-hoc extract the first balanced JSON object.
4. **Classify output.**
   - Contains `tool_calls[]` → validate each against its schema → dispatch → append `role:tool` messages → go to step 1 of next iteration.
   - Contains only `content` → emit as the final answer → `DONE`.
   - Malformed after repair attempts → enter fallback logic (§5).
5. **Guardrails.** Enforce max iterations, wall-clock deadline, and per-tool call quotas.

### 2.2 Tool-call format

The model emits an OpenAI/Gemini-style envelope (see `tools_definition.json`):

```json
{
  "tool_calls": [
    {"id":"call_1","type":"function",
     "function":{"name":"calculator","arguments":"{\"expression\":\"18*4+7\"}"}}
  ]
}
```

`arguments` is a **string** containing JSON — this matters because locally quantized models reliably emit strings, but often produce subtly invalid inner JSON. The router therefore applies a three-stage repair ladder before ever retrying the model (§4.2).

### 2.3 Tool result envelope

Every tool returns the same shape so the model sees one consistent observation grammar:

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "tool": "file_manager",
  "call_id": "call_1",
  "elapsed_ms": 42,
  "data": { "...": "tool-specific" },
  "error": null
}
```

Failure shape:

```json
{
  "ok": false, "tool": "web_search", "call_id": "call_2",
  "elapsed_ms": 30012,
  "error": {"code":"TIMEOUT","retriable":true,
            "message":"search backend exceeded 8000ms",
            "hint":"retry once, then narrow the query"}
}
```

The `retriable` and `hint` fields are the contract that drives the recovery loop — the model is instructed to *read the hint*, not to guess.

---

## 3. Token budget

The local model's context is finite (default configured at **4096 tokens**, overridable to 8192 for models that support it). Budget is a static allocation plus a dynamic remainder.

### 3.1 Static allocation (defaults for 4096-token context)

| Segment                                   | Allocated | Notes |
|-------------------------------------------|-----------|-------|
| System prompt (persona, rules, safety)    | 520       | Frozen; never truncated |
| Tool definitions (rendered)               | 430       | 4 tools ≈ 100 tok each |
| Output reserve (generation headroom)      | 700       | Never spent on input |
| Per-turn user message allowance           | 380       | Truncated with ellipsis beyond this |
| **Contingency / history remainder**       | **2066**  | Consumed by history + observations |

### 3.2 Dynamic rules

- `history_budget = context − (system + tools + output_reserve + current_user)`.
- Observations are stored **compressed**: tool results are truncated to `max_result_tokens` per tool (calculator: 64, settings: 96, file preview: 512, web search: 320 per result × max 5 results).
- **Truncation order (oldest first):** (1) tool result bodies → replaced by `«truncated: 4.1KB, head follows…»`; (2) old assistant reasoning; (3) older user turns beyond the 4-turn window. The system prompt and the newest user turn are never truncated.
- If after truncation the prompt still exceeds `context − output_reserve`, the loop short-circuits to `DONE` with a `CONTEXT_OVERFLOW` notice instead of feeding a sliced prompt to the model.
- Multi-step tasks put intermediate observations into a **scratchpad summary** rather than the full transcript: after 3 tool calls, the orchestrator asks the model for a one-line `plan_state` string that replaces the raw calls in history.

### 3.3 Budget telemetry

Each iteration logs `prompt_tokens`, `completion_tokens`, `headroom`. If headroom < 15% for two consecutive turns, the orchestrator proactively collapses history.

---

## 4. Error recovery loop

### 4.1 Error taxonomy

| Class | Examples | Strategy |
|-------|----------|----------|
| **A — Argument/schema errors** | missing `expression`, wrong type, unparseable JSON | Repair locally (§4.2); if unrepairable, one model re-prompt |
| **B — Retriable runtime errors** | `TIMEOUT`, `NETWORK_UNAVAILABLE`, `RATE_LIMITED`, `LOCK_BUSY` | Bounded retry with exponential backoff + jitter |
| **C — Semantic/permission errors** | `PATH_OUTSIDE_SANDBOX`, `SETTING_NOT_ALLOWED`, `DIVISION_BY_ZERO`, `NO_RESULTS` | **No retry.** Return actionable error + hint; model must change strategy |
| **D — Fatal** | `TOOL_DISABLED`, `MODEL_OOM`, `PANIC` | Abort loop, fall back per §5 |

### 4.2 Argument-repair ladder (runs before any model re-prompt)

1. Parse `arguments` as JSON → OK, dispatch.
2. Strip trailing commas / smart quotes / control chars → re-parse.
3. Extract first balanced `{…}` substring → re-parse.
4. Field-level coercion: numbers-as-strings → numbers, `"true"` → `true`, single-quote JSON → double-quote.
5. Still failing → **one** targeted model re-prompt: *"Your tool call for `{name}` failed validation: `{errors}`. Emit only corrected JSON arguments."* Budget: 200 tokens.
6. Second failure on the same call → classify D, go to fallback.

### 4.3 Retry policy

- **B-class only**, `max_attempts = 3` (configurable per tool in `agent_config.yaml`).
- Backoff: `base_delay * 2^(attempt-1) + jitter(0..250ms)`; capped by both `per_tool_retry_budget_ms` and the global wall-clock deadline.
- **Retry must differ:** attempt 2 may not be byte-identical to attempt 1 for `web_search` — the router appends a query refinement (drop stopwords, shorten) so identical failing requests are not repeated.
- Circuit breaker: after `circuit_breaker_threshold` consecutive B-class failures, the tool is marked *unhealthy* for `circuit_breaker_cooldown_ms`; subsequent calls short-circuit to `TOOL_UNHEALTHY` (class D) without touching the backend.

### 4.4 Loop diagram

```
model output
   │
   ├─ tool_calls ──► validate args
   │                    ├─ ok ──► dispatch(timeout)
   │                    │            ├─ ok ────► observation ──► next iteration
   │                    │            ├─ B error ► retry (≤3, backoff) ─► observation
   │                    │            ├─ C error ► observation with hint ─► next iteration
   │                    │            └─ D error ► FALLBACK (§5)
   │                    └─ invalid ─► repair ladder ─► re-prompt (×1) ─► FALLBACK
   ├─ content ────────► DONE
   └─ unparseable ────► re-prompt (×1) ─► FALLBACK
```

---

## 5. Fallback logic

Escalating, cheapest-first:

1. **Tool-level fallback (F1).** `web_search` fails class B after retries → serve the on-device cached corpus / `file_manager` search over downloaded documents; return `data.degraded = true` so the model can tell the user results may be stale.
2. **Strategy fallback (F2).** Tool returns class C (e.g. `NO_RESULTS`) → re-invoke once with a broadened or narrowed argument set (query synonyms, wider file glob). Max 1 broadening attempt per user turn.
3. **Model fallback (F3).** Primary model times out (`model_timeout_ms`) or returns garbage twice → switch to the tiny fallback model (or a deterministic intent+slot template parser) that maps intents directly to tool calls without free-form reasoning. Template routes: *calculate → calculator*, *find/open file → file_manager*, *turn on/off/adjust X → settings_manager*, *what is/search → web_search*.
4. **Tool disablement fallback (F4).** If a tool is unhealthy, the system prompt is regenerated with that tool removed and the model is told in one line which capability is missing, so it can offer alternatives rather than hallucinate a result.
5. **Surface fallback (F5).** Everything else fails → deterministic reply with the partial observations gathered so far, an explicit failure reason, and a retry affordance in the UI.
6. **Safety stop (F0, highest precedence).** Any write operation that is irreversible (`file_manager.delete`, `settings_manager.factory_reset`) requires a confirmation turn; if confirmation parsing fails twice, the operation is *cancelled*, never guessed.

Every fallback level is logged with `fallback_level` so evals can measure degradation distribution per model and per device class.

---

## 6. Tool-specific routing notes

- **`calculator`** — highest priority for anything that looks numeric; pure function, no I/O, timeout 1500 ms, never retried for class C (a math error is a model error, not a runtime error). Expression is evaluated by a whitelisted AST walker (no `eval`).
- **`file_manager`** — all paths resolved against a sandbox root (`/sdcard/Documents/AgentSandbox` by default); traversal (`..`), symlink escapes, and absolute paths outside the root are rejected as class C *before* any I/O.
- **`settings_manager`** — whitelist-only. Read-only keys are free; write keys require a capability token issued by the confirmation flow. Android privileged APIs are proxied through a companion `AccessibilityService`/`DeviceAdmin` bridge; absence of that bridge degrades to `READ_ONLY`.
- **`web_search`** — the only network tool. Network permission may be revoked at runtime; the router checks `ConnectivityManager` before dispatch to convert an inevitable timeout into an instant, cheap class C `NETWORK_UNAVAILABLE`.

---

## 7. Observability and evaluation

- Structured log per turn: `{turn, state, prompt_tokens, tool, args_hash, attempt, error_code, elapsed_ms, fallback_level}`.
- Golden-set routing eval (≥200 utterances) run on every prompt or schema change; pass criterion: ≥95% top-1 tool selection accuracy, 0 class-D leaks on calculator/file/settings.
- Fault-injection harness in `mock_tool_dispatcher.py` (`--fault` flags) exercises timeout, malformed-output, permission-denied, and circuit-breaker paths without a device.
